newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan plans to abolish its security council.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan plans to abolish its security council.

text.p: A close aide to Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif was on Wednesday quoted as saying the government would abolish a three-month-old national security council that had tilted power towards the presidency and the military.

Sharif's adviser on law and human rights, Khalid Anwar, was quoted by the national daily The News as saying President Farooq Leghari and the military would no longer be interested in the continuation of the controversial body.

His remarks in an interview followed a unanimous passage of landmark constitutional amendments by parliament on Tuesday that stripped the president of vital powers of sacking governments and appointing armed forces chiefs and provincial governors.

Anwar said the 10-member council, which Leghari set up with the approval of a caretaker government he named after sacking prime minister Benazir Bhutto in November, had neither a constitutional role nor did Sharif's six-week-old government have any plans to give it one.
"Rather we will abolish it by amending the rules of business," he said.
Sharif had declined to give specific comment on the issue when asked by reporters on Tuesday.

The 10-member Council for Defence and National Security, set up by a presidential order in January, included the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff committee and the army, navy and air force chiefs, as well as the prime minister and the ministers for defence, foreign affairs, interior and finance.

The president, supreme commander of the armed forces, chaired the council, which was empowered to advise on defence and national security issues and on economic and financial policies affecting them. It could also make recommendations on internal security matters and the proclamation of an emergency.
The president could refer any issue to the council without consulting the prime minister, in a potentially significant accretion of presidential power at the premier's expense.

In theory, the council's advice was not binding, but political analysts had said that given the already powerful influence of the military in Pakistani politics, it would seem hard for a prime minister to defy it.
